item.title: A case for food fortification with vitamin B12 in India
item.dc:creator: Abey Sushan
item.description:
The Indian Council of Medical Research–National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) has released findings from its 2023–25 SAMPADA survey, analyzing over 1.7 lakh venous blood samples across 183 districts—a crucial dataset designed to fill the gap left when anaemia indicators were excluded from the NFHS-6 fact sheets earlier this year. The headline prevalence figures remain sobering: 55.9% of non-pregnant women aged 15–49 and 46.3% of adolescent girls are anaemic. Yet the real epidemiological story lies in the etiology breakdown: only about 27% of anaemia cases involve iron deficiency, while roughly two-thirds of Indian adolescents (66.1% of boys and 65.4% of girls) and 63.1% of pregnant women are deficient in vitamin B12.

For public health programmes, this is an inflection point. Blanket iron–folic acid supplementation under initiatives like Anaemia Mukt Bharat inevitably hits an epidemiological ceiling when nearly three-quarters of anaemia is not driven by iron deficiency and widespread B12 depletion—alongside underlying hemoglobinopathies and chronic inflammation—goes unaddressed. Simply intensifying iron distribution will not move the needle further and risks unnecessary iron loading in non-deficient individuals; the next phase of India’s anaemia strategy must shift from presumptive mass supplementation to primary-care diagnostic triage, dietary diversification, and targeted B12 intervention.

item.title: Why Kerala’s crackdown on unregulated cosmetics and supplements matter
item.dc:creator: Abey Sushan
item.description: In a hospital ward, medicine begins with the patient in front of you. Recently, in Malappuram, that patient was a 17-year-old girl who developed severe swelling and heavy protein loss in her urine. The clinical diagnosis was secondary membranous nephropathy—a serious kidney disorder in which the organ’s delicate filtering membranes are damaged by immune complexes. The trigger was not an infection or an autoimmune flare. It was a jar of fairness cream bought online after being promoted on Instagram. When an accredited laboratory analysed the cream, it was found to contain 1.25 per cent mercury—12,500 parts per million. India’s Cosmetics Rules permit no more than 1 ppm as an unavoidable trace impurity. She had been applying a neurotoxic, nephrotoxic heavy metal to her skin at 12,500 times the legal limit. Cases like hers—and similar accounts now surfacing publicly from other users—expose a familiar public health problem: clinical teams are left treating preventable organ damage because regulation stopped where modern commerce begins. Following the Malappuram case, the Kerala Health Department’s move to frame strict guidelines—mandating formal licensing and registration for all offline and online cosmetics and protein supplements. Treating a 17-year-old with mercury-induced kidney disease and helping her recover is good clinical medicine. Closing the regulatory loopholes so the next five hundred teenagers never apply 12,500 ppm of mercury to their skin is public health.

item.title: Lessons from the recent loss of measles elimination status by the US
item.dc:creator: Abey Sushan
item.description:
The Pan American Health Organization’s November 17, 2026 decision to revoke the United States’ measles-elimination status marks a profound, self-inflicted failure in modern public health. Held continuously since 2000, that designation collapsed after the same viral lineage circulated uninterrupted for more than twelve months. By November 2026, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had confirmed 5,412 cases across nearly every state—more than double 2025’s tally and the highest national burden since 1991—alongside 48 outbreaks, multiple deaths, over 160 infections in pregnant women since 2025, and 13 cases of congenital measles. Escalating outbreaks in West Texas, South Carolina, and Pennsylvania exposed a sobering reality: biological elimination without institutional vigilance is entirely reversible.

Epidemiologically, this resurgence reflects the unforgiving mathematics of herd immunity. Because measles is among the most contagious human pathogens, preventing sustained transmission requires at least 95% population immunity via two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, which confers roughly 97% protection. Over recent years, U.S. kindergarten MMR coverage slipped from 95.2% to approximately 92.4%–92.7%, driven by expanding non-medical exemptions. National averages further obscured dangerous geographic clustering, where pockets of under-immunized communities acted as dry tinder for imported cases. Consequently, infants too young for their first dose and immunocompromised individuals lost the protective shield of community immunity, paying the highest price for others’ vaccine refusal. Rather than swiftly extinguishing sparks through aggressive ring vaccination and contact tracing, overwhelmed local health departments watched isolated clusters coalesce into sustained, multi-state endemic transmission.

Politically and institutionally, the American setback is an indictment of fragmented governance and legitimized vaccine skepticism. Public health specialists have rightly criticized federal health leadership under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for amplifying doubts about immunization safety and eroding public trust when unequivocal scientific messaging was essential. Allowing broad philosophical exemptions and weakening school-entry enforcement hollowed out decades of bipartisan public health consensus. Simultaneously, years of chronic underfunding left county health departments lacking surge epidemiologists and real-time surveillance capacity. While the CDC’s late-2026 allocation of $100 million to state and local jurisdictions acknowledges the emergency, reactive spending cannot instantly repair dismantled community trust. The United States proved that world-class biomedical innovation fails when misinformation outpaces primary prevention.

For India and Kerala, the American experience offers an urgent warning against public health complacency. Under its National Zero Measles-Rubella Elimination Campaign, India has pushed national coverage above 90%—reaching 93.7% for the first dose and 92.2% for the second—yet still recorded over 15,200 cases between April and September 2026, proving that high aggregate numbers cannot offset district-level immunity gaps. Even Kerala, despite its celebrated primary healthcare indicators, witnessed a deadly outbreak in Malappuram in September 2026 exceeding 100 cases and claiming young lives, where two-dose MR completion lagged around 63% to 70%. Both national and state systems must treat elimination as a continuous operational discipline: tracking cohort immunization down to the panchayat and block levels to sustain over 95% coverage, integrating digital registries with catch-up micro-planning to reach missed-dose children before imported transmission takes root, and engaging trusted local physicians and community leaders to counter digital misinformation early.

item.title: A space for musings on public health practice
item.dc:creator: Abey Sushan
item.description:
This space is created as a place for me to explore areas and topics I find interesting. It may sometimes be a rant on a specific topic. It may just be a note on something interesting I noticed. It will mostly be about the public health landscape of Kerala, India and the world. It can be about other things too.

Over time, this space may evolve into a chronicling of my journey in public health.

Note

This space is not intended to be educational.
